picks.tradeoff: Check required advanced procedures and current platform packages before standardizing on it.

recipes.title: Select astronomical camera capture software
recipes.description: Capture the night sky with software matched to the camera, driver, platform and observing workflow. High-frame-rate planetary video, live stacking and unattended deep-sky sequencing are distinct tasks.

picks.label: Private planetary acquisition
picks.reason: Focuses on supported astronomical cameras and planetary capture controls.
picks.tradeoff: The license prohibits commercial use, and camera support varies by operating system.

picks.label: Multi-platform supported-camera capture
picks.reason: Provides acquisition packages for Windows, Mac and Linux processor combinations.
picks.tradeoff: ChromeOS support ended; verify the precise camera SDK and architecture.

picks.label: Windows live stacking and EAA
picks.reason: Combines camera acquisition with live image accumulation and optional alignment tools.
picks.tradeoff: Selected functions require annual Pro licensing; unlicensed real-camera Pro testing disables saving.

picks.label: Deep-sky equipment and sequence coordination
picks.reason: Organizes supported equipment, targets, framing and imaging sequences on Windows.
picks.tradeoff: It serves a different acquisition pattern from planetary video; hardware and plugin compatibility must be checked.

recipes.title: Process astronomy captures for an image or measurement
recipes.description: Select visual image production or quantitative photometry first, and preserve the calibration data and processing history needed to assess the result.

picks.label: Calibration, registration and stacking
picks.reason: Provides an astrophotography processing workflow for prepared image sequences.
picks.tradeoff: Calibration frames, rejection settings and color handling influence the output.

picks.label: Astronomical image measurement
picks.reason: Provides calibration and photometry-oriented analysis derived from ImageJ.
picks.tradeoff: Quantitative measurements need appropriate apertures, reference stars and uncertainty checks.

picks.label: Plate solving and FITS inspection
picks.reason: Combines astrometric solving with stacking and related astronomy utilities.
picks.tradeoff: Required star databases and data preparation are separate installation concerns.

recipes.title: Choose a host for audio instruments and effects
recipes.description: Match plugin format, operating system, routing and stage-management requirements. Test the complete audio chain at the intended buffer size.

picks.label: Open plugin hosting and patching
picks.reason: Provides a dedicated host for loading and connecting instruments and effects.
picks.tradeoff: Plugin formats and optional bridges vary by build and operating system.

picks.label: Modular routing graph
picks.reason: Provides configurable audio/MIDI plugin graphs with free public builds.
picks.tradeoff: The no-charge channel trails paid update channels; hosted plugins need their own compatible licenses and binaries.

picks.label: Windows live performance management
picks.reason: Offers free basic VST hosting and paid set-list, routing and state tools.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced performance functions depend on edition; current releases require 64-bit Windows.

recipes.title: Convert an audio collection or extract CDs
recipes.description: Decide whether the target is archival lossless audio, portable listening copies or scripted conversion. Preserve source files when applying DSP or lossy encoding.

picks.label: Open desktop conversion and CD extraction
picks.reason: Combines audio conversion and disc extraction with supported encoders.
picks.tradeoff: Encoder and metadata options require deliberate setup for an archival workflow.

picks.label: Mac cue-sheet and lossless workflow
picks.reason: Provides lossless conversion, cue splitting and CD extraction with GUI and command-line routes.
picks.tradeoff: Mac only; the full source/package license set remains unresolved in this review.

picks.label: Commercial library conversion interface
picks.reason: Provides batch filtering, file-manager integration and CD-ripping tools.
picks.tradeoff: The trial is time-limited, some codec/automation options are Windows-only, and the full EULA remains a research gap.

picks.label: Scripted multimedia transformations
picks.reason: Provides explicit codec and filter commands suitable for reproducible batches.
picks.tradeoff: The command line demands precise stream and format choices; a successful command can still produce an unintended quality change.

recipes.title: Choose language annotation or acoustic measurement tools
recipes.description: Distinguish labeling what happened in a recording from measuring the acoustic signal. Many research projects need both and an explicit interchange workflow.

picks.label: Hierarchical multimodal annotation
picks.reason: Synchronizes audio/video with time-aligned tiers, controlled vocabularies and structured EAF documents.
picks.tradeoff: Playback depends on codecs and platform; tier design and annotation agreement need their own protocol.

picks.label: Phonetic signal measurements
picks.reason: Provides speech-oriented acoustic analysis and scripting alongside annotation.
picks.tradeoff: Pitch/formant parameters and segmentation choices affect measurements.

picks.label: Layered audio inspection
picks.reason: Combines spectrograms, annotation and available analysis layers for detailed review.
picks.tradeoff: It does not replace a corpus annotation scheme or a validated phonetic measurement method.

recipes.title: Choose a desktop globe or GIS workspace
recipes.description: Choose visual geographic context versus data processing. Imagery access, content rights and project formats determine long-term portability.

picks.label: Open virtual-globe exploration
picks.reason: Provides map themes and globe-based geographic exploration.
picks.tradeoff: Available map sources have different coverage and rights.

picks.label: Google imagery and KML context
picks.reason: Provides desktop imagery exploration, historical views and GIS import/export.
picks.tradeoff: Desktop downloads end on 25 June 2027; imagery attribution and bulk-download restrictions still apply.

picks.label: Data editing and spatial analysis
picks.reason: Provides a full GIS workbench for local layers and processing.
picks.tradeoff: It needs explicitly sourced datasets; it does not automatically include the same imagery service.

recipes.title: Prepare or maintain an annotated phylogenetic tree figure
recipes.description: These viewers present already inferred trees. Inspect rooting, branch units, metadata and uncertainty before making a publication figure.

picks.label: Current FigTree successor
picks.reason: Combines tree/metadata display and export with desktop packages and local browser operation.
picks.tradeoff: Temporal interpretations require valid dates and models; the viewer does not establish inference quality.

picks.label: Legacy figure compatibility
picks.reason: Can reproduce an existing FigTree-based presentation workflow.
picks.tradeoff: The upstream README says PearTree supersedes it; ongoing FigTree support is not assumed.

recipes.title: Measure motion from video and analyze the resulting data
recipes.description: Choose a calibrated physics-video workflow for trajectories, image analysis for pixel/region measurements, and a plotting tool for exported data. These stages are complementary.

picks.label: Calibrated trajectory and model comparison
picks.reason: Tracks objects, overlays vectors and compares particle models against recorded motion.
picks.tradeoff: Perspective, frame timing and calibration errors propagate into velocity and acceleration; test the actual video format.

picks.label: Image and region analysis
picks.reason: Provides a plugin-based scientific image-analysis environment for supported image sequences.
picks.tradeoff: A suitable method/plugin and calibration are needed; not every image workflow is a physics trajectory measurement.

picks.label: Inspect and fit exported measurements
picks.reason: Combines data import, plotting and fitting after acquisition.
picks.tradeoff: The plotting stage cannot recover missing calibration or correct an invalid tracking model.

recipes.title: Test browser flows and reproduce interface failures
recipes.description: Choose the browser control and debugging model that matches the task. Supported engines do not make desktop emulation equivalent to a physical mobile device.

picks.label: Cross-engine application tests
picks.reason: Isolated contexts, auto-waiting assertions and trace inspection support repeatable flows across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
picks.tradeoff: Browser binaries and system dependencies must be installed; physical device testing remains separate.

picks.label: Interactive test development
picks.reason: The visible runner shows the application alongside test command history during component and end-to-end test development.
picks.tradeoff: Its execution model differs from WebDriver, and hosted Cloud features have separate plans.

picks.label: Scripted browser tasks
picks.reason: A direct browser API suits page rendering, PDF generation, screenshots and custom automation helpers.
picks.tradeoff: It is a programming library; assertions, test organization and reporting need additional choices.

picks.label: Readable acceptance workflows
picks.reason: Reusable keywords can connect browser actions to broader application acceptance steps.
picks.tradeoff: Automation capabilities come from libraries, each with its own prerequisites and support scope.

recipes.title: Design realistic service load tests
recipes.description: Workload design and load-generator capacity determine whether results answer the intended question. These selections reflect scripting and protocol needs, not a benchmark ranking.

picks.label: JavaScript workload scenarios
picks.reason: Scenarios, thresholds and metric exports suit versioned performance checks in development pipelines.
picks.tradeoff: Local execution needs sufficient resources; optional Grafana Cloud services are priced separately.

picks.label: Python user behavior
picks.reason: Python tasks and distributed workers suit custom user journeys and reuse of existing Python helpers.
picks.tradeoff: The test code and generator capacity need profiling so they do not become the bottleneck.

picks.label: Protocol-rich test plans
picks.reason: A GUI plan editor and a broad sampler ecosystem help assemble tests involving multiple service protocols.
picks.tradeoff: Generate substantial load in command-line mode and budget the Java runtime and plugin overhead.

picks.label: Controlled HTTP request rates
picks.reason: A CLI/library model supports repeatable HTTP workloads at a specified request rate with exported results.
picks.tradeoff: Complex multi-step user behavior requires additional scripting or another workload model.

picks.label: Quick terminal HTTP checks
picks.reason: A standalone command-line interface with live terminal feedback suits focused endpoint experiments.
picks.tradeoff: A short endpoint test is not a complete simulation of a production service workload.

recipes.title: Develop against predictable API responses
recipes.description: A mock server supplies controlled behavior; a request checker verifies it. Combine these roles when a remote dependency is unavailable or difficult to reproduce.

picks.label: Design mocks visually
picks.reason: The desktop editor provides routes, templating and response rules for local mock API servers.
picks.tradeoff: Centralized collaboration and managed deployments belong to separately licensed Pro offerings.

picks.label: Programmatic stubs and scenarios
picks.reason: Request matching, stateful scenarios and a standalone Java server suit repository-managed service test fixtures.
picks.tradeoff: A compatible Java runtime and deliberate stub design are required.

picks.label: Assert request and response behavior
picks.reason: Text files can chain HTTP requests, extract values and check responses in CI.
picks.tradeoff: Hurl sends and checks requests; it does not replace the server providing mocked responses.

picks.label: Maintain interactive API collections
picks.reason: Local collection files support manual API exploration and review in version control.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced or team capabilities can require a paid edition.

recipes.title: Find Python CPU and memory bottlenecks
recipes.description: Choose the measurement question first: sampling a running process, attributing CPU/memory work to lines, or explaining allocation stacks.

picks.label: Sample a running Python process
picks.reason: An external sampling profiler can inspect Python execution and generate flame graphs without rewriting application code.
picks.tradeoff: Process inspection may need additional privileges; samples do not enumerate every allocation.

picks.label: Separate Python and native work
picks.reason: Line-oriented CPU and memory reporting helps locate Python code, native code and allocation activity in one report.
picks.tradeoff: GPU reporting depends on supported hardware; optional AI suggestions need separate correctness review.

picks.label: Explain allocation growth
picks.reason: Native and Python allocation stacks, reports and flame graphs help investigate memory use and leaks.
picks.tradeoff: The supported host set is Linux and macOS; wheels and native dependencies must match the environment.

recipes.title: Inspect native and JVM performance profiles
recipes.description: Sampling, allocation instrumentation and JVM inspection answer different questions. Capture representative workloads with symbols and permissions appropriate to the selected tool.

picks.label: Capture across desktop systems
picks.reason: Sampling on Windows, macOS and Linux can feed an interactive Firefox Profiler interface.
picks.tradeoff: Event support and collection permissions differ by operating system.

picks.label: Explore Linux perf recordings
picks.reason: Call trees, source/assembly views and flame graphs help interpret Linux perf data in a GUI.
picks.tradeoff: The capture and debug symbols must be usable; the collection workflow is Linux-focused.

picks.label: Trace JVM and native stacks
picks.reason: Profiling JVM workloads with native stack visibility suits CPU, allocation and lock investigations.
picks.tradeoff: Linux and macOS support depends on JVM, event and operating-system configuration.

picks.label: Inspect a running Java application
picks.reason: A desktop interface brings JVM monitoring, thread/heap inspection and profiling tools together.
picks.tradeoff: Connection configuration and JDK compatibility matter; deep profiling can change workload behavior.

picks.label: Investigate native memory correctness
picks.reason: Instrumentation tools such as Memcheck and Massif help explain memory errors and heap usage.
picks.tradeoff: Execution can slow substantially, supported OS/CPU combinations are limited, and upstream provides source releases.

recipes.title: Make project runtimes and environments reproducible
recipes.description: A runtime-version manager and a dependency/environment manager control different parts of a workstation. Pick by language and native-library needs.

picks.label: Python packages and environments
picks.reason: Python version management, project lockfiles and isolated tool execution provide a cohesive Python workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Native package dependencies and indexes still need compatible builds and deliberate trust choices.

picks.label: Python plus native libraries
picks.reason: Conda and PyPI dependencies, lockfiles and project tasks suit scientific or mixed native/Python environments.
picks.tradeoff: Available packages and solver results depend on the selected channels and target platforms.

picks.label: Several language tool versions
picks.reason: Per-project runtime versions, environment configuration and tasks suit polyglot development.
picks.tradeoff: Backend and plugin support differs across tools and operating systems.

picks.label: Focused Node.js switching
picks.reason: A dedicated Node.js version manager supports automatic project version selection.
picks.tradeoff: Shell initialization is required; JavaScript package dependencies are a separate concern.

picks.label: Native Windows Python selection
picks.reason: A Windows-specific implementation supplies the Python version-switching workflow that Unix pyenv does not provide natively.
picks.tradeoff: Available versions and shell/path configuration differ from the original pyenv project.

recipes.title: Improve native build and test feedback
recipes.description: Configure the build graph first, then decide whether execution, caching or test scheduling is the limiting factor. Cache tools do not guarantee a speedup for every project.

picks.label: Generate project build systems
picks.reason: Platform and toolchain abstractions connect a source project to IDEs and build backends.
picks.tradeoff: Complex cross-compilation and dependency discovery still require project-specific configuration.

picks.label: Describe builds declaratively
picks.reason: A focused build-definition language and dependency discovery suit new native projects with a supported toolchain.
picks.tradeoff: Migrating an existing build can be substantial, and backend behavior must match project needs.

picks.label: Execute a generated build graph
picks.reason: A small build executor runs commands from a dependency graph generated by another tool.
picks.tradeoff: It does not replace a higher-level project configurator such as CMake or Meson.

picks.label: Reuse C/C++ compilation results
picks.reason: Repeated compatible compiler invocations can use local or configured remote cached results.
picks.tradeoff: Changing relevant inputs or using unsupported compilation modes causes misses or bypasses.

picks.label: Share Rust and C/C++ compilation caches
picks.reason: Multiple storage backends and optional distributed compilation suit teams with compatible repeated builds.
picks.tradeoff: Remote storage, credentials and cache compatibility add setup and maintenance work.

picks.label: Schedule Rust test binaries
picks.reason: Isolated test processes, filtering and profiles provide control over large Rust test suites.
picks.tradeoff: Doctests require the standard Cargo workflow; concurrency and isolation can expose test assumptions.

recipes.title: Explore local data and share queryable results
recipes.description: Choose a query engine, terminal interface or publishing layer according to where the data lives and who needs to use it.

picks.label: Query analytical files in process
picks.reason: SQL over formats such as CSV and Parquet supports local analytical work without deploying a separate database server.
picks.tradeoff: It is not a drop-in substitute for a multi-user transactional service.

picks.label: Work in a terminal SQL interface
picks.reason: An editor, query results and database adapters make interactive SQL practical in a terminal.
picks.tradeoff: Capabilities depend on the adapter, driver and terminal environment.

picks.label: Convert and reshape SQLite data
picks.reason: A CLI and Python library support imports, schema changes and SQL over local SQLite databases.
picks.tradeoff: It is script-oriented and SQLite-focused rather than a full visual administration suite.

picks.label: Browse and publish SQLite content
picks.reason: A local web interface and JSON endpoints expose queryable data to other users and tools.
picks.tradeoff: Deployment, permissions and exposed data require deliberate configuration.

picks.label: Inspect many tabular formats
picks.reason: Keyboard-driven sheets support sorting, filtering and exploration before or alongside SQL work.
picks.tradeoff: Large data still consumes memory; its Windows route uses WSL rather than a native build.

recipes.title: Evaluate and script language-model workflows
recipes.description: Select an evaluator, command-line client or serving runtime by role. Local tools can still incur provider charges and send data externally when configured to use remote services.

picks.label: Compare prompts on a test suite
picks.reason: Versioned cases, assertions and provider comparisons help detect changes in a defined model workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Test design and graders determine what is measured; passing a suite does not establish broad safety or correctness.

picks.label: Keep model calls scriptable
picks.reason: A CLI, plugin ecosystem and response logging suit repeatable model calls in shell workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Providers, plugins and models have separate setup, licensing and cost considerations.

picks.label: Use several providers from a terminal
picks.reason: Chat, retrieval and tool-oriented terminal workflows can share one configured client.
picks.tradeoff: Provider credentials, external data transfer and tool execution need deliberate configuration.

picks.label: Serve supported models on Linux
picks.reason: Continuous batching and a server API suit controlled local or on-premises model serving.
picks.tradeoff: GPU/CPU support, memory needs and deployment tuning are substantial; Windows support is through WSL.

picks.label: Start with a desktop local-model interface
picks.reason: Model discovery, chat and a local server provide a graphical path to supported local models.
picks.tradeoff: The app is proprietary, model licenses vary, and current macOS builds require Apple Silicon.

recipes.title: Choose a tool for a small original game
recipes.description: Match the authoring model and target first: a broad engine, event-based visual logic, a Lua framework, retro constraints or a narrative-first workflow.

picks.label: Integrated 2D and 3D authoring
picks.reason: A scene editor, scripting and export workflow support a range of original game projects.
picks.tradeoff: Target exports and advanced rendering features have platform-specific requirements.

picks.label: Event-based visual logic
picks.reason: A visual event system and editor help create games without starting from a code-only framework.
picks.tradeoff: Hosted build, publishing and collaboration allowances differ between free and paid plans.

picks.label: Lua and component-based projects
picks.reason: An integrated editor and Lua scripting support focused cross-platform 2D/3D production.
picks.tradeoff: The custom source-available license restricts commercialization of the engine/editor itself.

picks.label: Code-oriented 2D games
picks.reason: A Lua framework supplies graphics, audio and input while leaving game structure to the programmer.
picks.tradeoff: There is no integrated scene editor, and packaging remains part of the development work.

picks.label: Game Boy-style constraints
picks.reason: Visual scripting and retro asset workflows produce games for the supported Game Boy and web targets.
picks.tradeoff: Hardware-style limits, asset rules and engine constraints shape the design.

picks.label: Visual novels and dialogue
picks.reason: A narrative-focused engine combines dialogue scripts, branching, saves and presentation features.
picks.tradeoff: General action or 3D games usually need a more suitable engine or extensive custom work.

recipes.title: Choose a modding tool by game asset format
recipes.description: Identify the engine and asset type before choosing a tool. Format support, game-specific encryption and export limitations matter more than an overall popularity ranking.

picks.label: Inspect supported Unreal assets
picks.reason: Package browsing and previews help inspect supported Unreal Engine game content.
picks.tradeoff: The Windows tool requires compatible mappings or keys for some games and cannot make every custom format readable.

picks.label: Recover supported Unity content
picks.reason: Asset extraction and project reconstruction workflows help inspect supported Unity data.
picks.tradeoff: Recovered projects may need repairs; some analysis/export capabilities require Premium.

picks.label: Modify Unity asset bundles
picks.reason: Type and bundle editing suits deliberate changes to supported Unity asset data.
picks.tradeoff: It is primarily a modding editor, and dependencies and newer game formats can impose limits.

picks.label: Inspect Bethesda NIF structures
picks.reason: The explicitly identified fo76utils fork adds newer-format rendering, materials and selected glTF workflows.
picks.tradeoff: It is experimental; format and import limitations differ by game, and the binary CPU requirements matter.

picks.label: Adjust supported body and outfit meshes
picks.reason: BodySlide and Outfit Studio provide slider, mesh-fitting and outfit-editing workflows for supported game setups.
picks.tradeoff: Correct game files, presets and skeleton/physics expectations are required; it is not a general-purpose 3D editor.

picks.label: Prepare DirectX textures
picks.reason: DDS conversion, mipmaps and block-compression options support game texture preparation.
picks.tradeoff: Color space, alpha behavior and compression must match the target; Windows imaging support differs from WSL builds.

recipes.title: Choose a browser for workspaces or keyboard control
recipes.description: Workspace organization, Firefox-derived customization and programmable keyboard navigation offer different ways to manage browsing. Compatibility and timely engine updates still need attention.

picks.label: Organize split views and workspaces
picks.reason: Vertical tabs, workspace organization and split views suit users keeping several related pages visible.
picks.tradeoff: Widevine DRM is unavailable on the documented Windows/macOS path, and workspaces alone do not isolate all browser data.

picks.label: Customize a Firefox-derived workspace
picks.reason: Sidebar and layout controls provide several ways to arrange pages and browser functions.
picks.tradeoff: Customization adds settings to learn, and website compatibility still depends on the underlying browser stack.

picks.label: Use Firefox-derived desktop features
picks.reason: Private tabs and customization features provide a free desktop browsing alternative.
picks.tradeoff: Its smaller project and separate release process require checking current compatibility and security updates.

picks.label: Navigate primarily with a keyboard
picks.reason: Vim-style controls and Python configuration suit a minimal keyboard-oriented interface.
picks.tradeoff: QtWebEngine packaging influences codecs and updates; normal Firefox/Chrome extension support is not provided.

picks.label: Program the browsing workflow
picks.reason: Lisp configuration and keyboard-oriented commands suit users who want extensive programmable browser behavior.
picks.tradeoff: GNU/Linux is the primary supported path; macOS and Windows are in development, and the interface requires learning.

recipes.title: Choose an editor for your programming workflow
recipes.description: Match graphical tooling, terminal habits, and licensing preferences. These are workflow choices based on documented features, not measured speed rankings.

picks.label: Broad graphical tooling
picks.reason: Integrated debugging, terminals, source control, and extensions support many languages in one workspace.
picks.tradeoff: The official Microsoft binary has different terms from the MIT-licensed Code-OSS source; extensions have their own licenses.

picks.label: Custom terminal workflow
picks.reason: Lua configuration and an embeddable API suit users who want to assemble a keyboard-driven environment.
picks.tradeoff: Modal editing and plugin configuration require learning and ongoing choices.

picks.label: Integrated terminal features
picks.reason: Multiple selections, Tree-sitter editing, and built-in LSP support provide a cohesive terminal editing model.
picks.tradeoff: Its selection-first controls differ from Vim and GUI editors.

picks.label: Paid text-editing focus
picks.reason: Multiple selections and project navigation suit intensive text manipulation in a graphical editor.
picks.tradeoff: Continued use requires a paid license, and deeper IDE features can require plugins.

recipes.title: Pick a Python workspace for learning or analysis
recipes.description: A debugger for learning, an interactive scientific IDE, and notebooks solve different problems.

picks.label: Learn program execution
picks.reason: Its teaching-focused debugger exposes expression evaluation and variable state.
picks.tradeoff: Larger multi-language projects may need a broader development environment.

picks.label: Inspect scientific variables
picks.reason: An IPython console and variable explorer support array and dataframe investigation beside scripts.
picks.tradeoff: Scientific dependencies and environment selection must be kept consistent.

picks.label: Combine code and explanation
picks.reason: Notebooks keep narrative, code, outputs, and data exploration together.
picks.tradeoff: Kernel and execution-order state need discipline for reproducible results.

recipes.title: Review changes and manage Git history
recipes.description: Choose by operating system and preference for a terminal, a guided client, or deeper graphical history tools.

picks.label: Terminal Git workflow
picks.reason: Status, diffs, staging, branches, and rebasing remain accessible from a keyboard-driven interface.
picks.tradeoff: The visual interface does not remove the need to understand history-changing operations.

picks.label: Guided commits
picks.reason: Visual diffs and a focused commit workflow help users review what they are about to commit.
picks.tradeoff: Official distributions support Windows and macOS; advanced Git actions may need the CLI.

picks.label: Windows repository inspection
picks.reason: A commit graph, branch tools, and Windows integration support detailed repository work.
picks.tradeoff: Windows prerequisites and Git configuration still need setup.

picks.label: Paid desktop history tools
picks.reason: Visual interactive rebase, image diffs, and a merge helper suit users who want a dedicated Git GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Windows/macOS only, with a paid license following evaluation.

recipes.title: Build API collections or inspect live HTTP behavior
recipes.description: Sending a request, maintaining a test collection, and intercepting application traffic are distinct tasks.

picks.label: Version API collections
picks.reason: Local plain-text collections can live with the application repository and be reviewed in Git.
picks.tradeoff: Some advanced and team features belong to paid editions.

picks.label: Standalone request CLI
picks.reason: Concise request syntax and formatted responses suit quick terminal investigation.
picks.tradeoff: Not every HTTPie option or behavior is implemented.

picks.label: Inspect and replay traffic
picks.reason: An intercepting proxy with scripting supports repeatable HTTP debugging of authorized targets.
picks.tradeoff: HTTPS interception requires explicit certificate trust and deliberate target configuration.

picks.label: Visual application interception
picks.reason: Application integrations and request filtering help inspect supported HTTP clients through a GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced features and target integrations vary by plan and environment.

recipes.title: Inspect a local database or manage several engines
recipes.description: Start with the database engine and whether the task is browsing, querying, or administration.

picks.label: Local SQLite files
picks.reason: Visual tables and SQL execution let users inspect a SQLite file without a server.
picks.tradeoff: This is a SQLite-focused tool, not a multi-engine administration suite.

picks.label: Several database engines
picks.reason: Drivers, SQL editing, and data browsing share one cross-platform interface.
picks.tradeoff: Enterprise and cloud features can differ between Community and paid products.

picks.label: PostgreSQL administration
picks.reason: PostgreSQL-specific object and server tooling provides dedicated administrative context.
picks.tradeoff: It is specialized for PostgreSQL rather than every database engine.

picks.label: Integrated SQL development
picks.reason: Schema-aware SQL and interactive data tools suit database-centric development work.
picks.tradeoff: Free non-commercial eligibility and commercial subscriptions have different conditions.

recipes.title: Choose a local AI interface or inference runtime
recipes.description: Choose the model and memory budget first, then the interface and deployment control you need. No hardware benchmark or model-quality winner is claimed.

picks.label: Managed models and local API
picks.reason: Model management and an application-facing API simplify supported local-model workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Model memory needs, acceleration support, optional cloud use, and model licenses must be checked.

picks.label: Detailed runtime control
picks.reason: Explicit GGUF files and hardware backends suit users who want direct inference configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Build options and supported architectures require more technical decisions.

picks.label: Desktop chat interface
picks.reason: A graphical workspace offers local models alongside configured external providers.
picks.tradeoff: Privacy and cost depend on which provider and model are selected.

picks.label: Questions over documents
picks.reason: Document ingestion and retrieval can be organized into dedicated workspaces.
picks.tradeoff: A local installation can still send data to configured external embedding or model services.

recipes.title: Automate service flows or repetitive typing
recipes.description: Use a flow engine for events and integrations, and a desktop text expander for repeated text. These tools can be complementary.

picks.label: Event and device flows
picks.reason: Visual message flows and reusable nodes support service, API, and device integration.
picks.tradeoff: Installed nodes, credentials, and exposed endpoints require maintenance.

picks.label: Internal service workflows
picks.reason: Visual integration steps and custom code can be combined in hosted or self-hosted workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Its Sustainable Use and enterprise licenses are source-available, with restrictions beyond standard open-source licenses.

picks.label: Connector-based automation
picks.reason: Reusable pieces and visual flows support common service integrations.
picks.tradeoff: Community and enterprise portions use different licensing and features.

picks.label: Cross-application snippets
picks.reason: Typed triggers expand reusable text across supported desktop applications.
picks.tradeoff: Input permissions and application compatibility vary by operating system.

recipes.title: Choose tools for a modded game setup
recipes.description: Match the game and mod ecosystem before choosing a manager; an editor or conflict checker complements deployment rather than replacing it.

picks.label: Profiles and virtual files
picks.reason: Virtual-filesystem deployment separates managed mods from original files for supported games.
picks.tradeoff: Game support and a correct load order still need explicit verification.

picks.label: Nexus-centered workflows
picks.reason: Game extensions, deployment, and profiles integrate with supported Nexus Mods workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Extension support, filesystem requirements, and site account features vary.

picks.label: Isolated Minecraft instances
picks.reason: Separate instances organize Minecraft versions, loaders, Java settings, and modpacks.
picks.tradeoff: The game account and all selected Java, loader, and mod versions must be compatible.

picks.label: Bethesda record conflicts
picks.reason: Record-level views reveal plugin conflicts before creating a compatibility patch.
picks.tradeoff: This is a specialist editor; incorrect changes can damage a load order and require backups.

recipes.title: Choose an emulator for the console and title
recipes.description: Console coverage is the first filter. Then consult each project's game compatibility and setup documentation; game and firmware data are separate.

picks.label: GameCube and Wii
picks.reason: Controls and graphics configuration are specialized for GameCube and Wii software.
picks.tradeoff: Per-game compatibility and required controller behavior vary.

picks.label: PlayStation 2
picks.reason: PS2-specific configuration and rendering options support a large range of title-specific setups.
picks.tradeoff: A suitable BIOS and game data are required, and performance depends on the title and hardware.

picks.label: PlayStation 3
picks.reason: The project documents title compatibility and per-game configuration for PS3 emulation.
picks.tradeoff: Hardware demands are substantial for some titles; the official download page was blocked to this research environment.

picks.label: Unified multi-core frontend
picks.reason: A common interface shares controller and display configuration across compatible Libretro cores.
picks.tradeoff: Every core has separate compatibility and licensing; a frontend does not make all consoles equivalent.

recipes.title: Find the source of slow frames or expensive code
recipes.description: Match the measurement tool to the layer being investigated and use a reproducible workload.

picks.label: Rendering pipeline inspection
picks.reason: A captured frame exposes resource contents, shaders, and pipeline state for supported APIs.
picks.tradeoff: Use supported applications and APIs; upstream support is focused on programs you create.

picks.label: Instrumented native programs
picks.reason: CPU, memory, and synchronization events can be correlated on detailed timelines.
picks.tradeoff: Instrumentation needs integration and can influence the measured workload.

picks.label: Correlate system traces
picks.reason: Trace timelines and SQL analysis support multiple event sources in one investigation.
picks.tradeoff: System-wide recording is platform-specific; viewers and analysis tools have broader support.

picks.label: Inspect sampled stacks
picks.reason: Interactive profile views help examine expensive call paths in an imported profile.
picks.tradeoff: It is a viewer, so a separate profiler must first capture compatible data.

recipes.title: Choose a download tool for the transfer type
recipes.description: Select by protocol and automation needs, then use official sources and content you have permission to download.

picks.label: Automated resumable transfers
picks.reason: Several transfer protocols and an RPC interface suit scripted download queues.
picks.tradeoff: Remote-control interfaces need deliberate configuration and access protection.

picks.label: Desktop transfer queue
picks.reason: An aria2-based engine is exposed through a graphical queue.
picks.tradeoff: Site-specific logins or restrictions may need a different workflow.

picks.label: BitTorrent transfers
picks.reason: Desktop and optional web interfaces provide torrent management and transfer controls.
picks.tradeoff: Optional plugins and remote web access introduce additional configuration choices.

picks.label: Permitted media extraction
picks.reason: Site extractors, format selection, and FFmpeg integration support repeatable media workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Extractor compatibility changes with websites, and access rights remain separate from technical support.

recipes.title: Choose a browser by workflow and privacy needs
recipes.description: Browser engine, tab organization, defaults, and network routing are separate choices. No browser is claimed universally fastest or safest.

picks.label: Independent browser engine
picks.reason: Gecko and Firefox's extension ecosystem offer an alternative to Chromium-based products.
picks.tradeoff: Test required sites and extensions against the chosen browser and settings.

picks.label: Organize many web tasks
picks.reason: Tab workspaces, tiling, and panels support many concurrent websites in one interface.
picks.tradeoff: The full browser has proprietary terms and more configuration choices.

picks.label: Privacy-oriented defaults
picks.reason: A Firefox-derived configuration includes privacy settings and a content blocker.
picks.tradeoff: Stricter defaults and DRM choices can reduce compatibility with some sites.

picks.label: Tor routing and onion sites
picks.reason: The browser and Tor routing are configured together for a coordinated privacy workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Expect network and site-compatibility tradeoffs; extra plugins or identifying account use can undermine privacy.

recipes.title: Plan a project on your desktop
recipes.description: Choose by scheduling depth, file interchange and whether a text-based model is useful. These local planners do not imply the collaboration features of their separate cloud products.

picks.label: Local Gantt planning
picks.reason: Task dependencies, baselines and resource-load views cover everyday individual scheduling.
picks.tradeoff: Shared editing requires a separate collaboration arrangement.

picks.label: Critical path and cost controls
picks.reason: Desktop combines critical-path analysis, work breakdown, baselines and earned-value views.
picks.tradeoff: Validate imported Microsoft Project files; portfolio features belong to a separate cloud product.

picks.label: Constraint-driven text models
picks.reason: Declarative schedules can account for resource constraints and be regenerated from versioned source.
picks.tradeoff: Learning the scheduling language takes more effort than dragging a bar on a chart.

recipes.title: Schedule people across projects
recipes.description: Distinguish calculated capacity-aware scheduling from a shared timeline. Start with the real constraints and test a representative plan.

picks.label: Shared resource planning
picks.reason: Portfolio planning and capacity allocation are central to its documented project controls.
picks.tradeoff: A configured server and an agreed project process are necessary.

picks.label: Reproducible capacity model
picks.reason: Resource constraints and scheduling rules can be expressed as reviewable text.
picks.tradeoff: Technical modeling is required and collaborative editing is external.

picks.label: Shared work-package plans
picks.reason: Dependencies, work packages and project discussions live in one team service.
picks.tradeoff: Do not assume every enterprise scheduling or portfolio feature is in Community.

recipes.title: Run a self-hosted product backlog
recipes.description: Pick the workflow first: Scrum ceremonies, cycles and product documents, or configurable issue states.

picks.label: Scrum and Kanban teams
picks.reason: Backlogs, sprints, stories and burndown views follow familiar agile planning workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Several services must be deployed and maintained.

picks.label: Cycles and product context
picks.reason: Cycles, modules and pages connect planned work with product documentation.
picks.tradeoff: Edition limits and operational requirements need review.

picks.label: Configurable issue workflows
picks.reason: Custom fields, role controls, wikis and repository integrations suit structured project tracking.
picks.tradeoff: Ruby deployment and plugin compatibility require technical ownership.

recipes.title: Host your own Kanban boards
recipes.description: Compare board scope and licensing before committing a team or inviting external clients.

picks.label: Focused WIP workflow
picks.reason: A compact board with work-in-progress limits and event actions suits a deliberate small workflow.
picks.tradeoff: The project is explicitly in maintenance mode.

picks.label: Imports and broad board features
picks.reason: Swimlanes, custom fields, rules and imports support richer board organization.
picks.tradeoff: Its larger feature and deployment surface needs administration.

picks.label: Real-time internal collaboration
picks.reason: Cards, comments and attachments provide a direct shared board experience.
picks.tradeoff: Community terms restrict some external commercial and hosted uses; check the exact license.

recipes.title: Track personal tasks and time locally
recipes.description: These tools cover different parts of a personal workflow; select a visual task tree, a terminal task list, or interval tracking.

picks.label: Desktop task trees
picks.reason: Nested tasks and effort records keep detailed personal work in a local GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Use current package instructions because older website release text is stale.

picks.label: Automated terminal tasks
picks.reason: Filters, reports and hooks integrate task lists with shell workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Command syntax replaces a visual planning interface.

picks.label: Tagged time intervals
picks.reason: CLI timers, backfill and reports complement a Taskwarrior workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Team approvals and invoicing are separate concerns.

picks.label: Visual time timeline
picks.reason: Editable intervals, tags and PDF/CSV reports suit a personal or freelance timesheet.
picks.tradeoff: Running the local web service still takes setup.

recipes.title: Choose a self-hosted business system
recipes.description: Define accounting localization, stock processes and implementation capacity before selecting a general ERP. The guide compares documented scope rather than certifying regulatory compliance.

picks.label: Integrated business operations
picks.reason: Accounting, purchasing, inventory and manufacturing are available in one Frappe-based suite.
picks.tradeoff: Implementation and localization are substantial work.

picks.label: Modular small-business workflows
picks.reason: ERP and CRM modules can be introduced around the processes a smaller organization needs.
picks.tradeoff: Specialized modules and hosted services may have separate costs.

picks.label: Modular ERP with desktop client
picks.reason: A native client and browser access share modular accounting, stock and manufacturing services.
picks.tradeoff: The desktop client still requires an administered Tryton server.

picks.label: Community application ecosystem
picks.reason: The LGPL Community edition provides a base for integrated business applications.
picks.tradeoff: Enterprise-only modules and capabilities must be checked separately.

picks.label: Custom business foundations
picks.reason: A Java business framework supports teams developing their own operational applications.
picks.tradeoff: This is an implementation project, not a turnkey accounting download.

recipes.title: Manage parts, assets or expiring stock
recipes.description: Inventory software is specialized: components, assigned IT equipment and warehouse lots represent different records and transactions.

picks.label: Components and assemblies
picks.reason: Parts, BOMs, suppliers and build stock connect component availability to assembly work.
picks.tradeoff: Financial accounting and retail checkout are separate systems.

picks.label: Electronics bench inventory
picks.reason: Datasheets, component parameters, labels and KiCad integration suit electronic parts.
picks.tradeoff: External suppliers or AI services may have their own access and pricing terms.

picks.label: Assigned IT equipment
picks.reason: Check-in/check-out records show who holds equipment, licenses and accessories.
picks.tradeoff: It is an asset register rather than a warehouse fulfillment system.

picks.label: Lots and warehouse movements
picks.reason: Facilities, shipments, lot identifiers and expiry dates fit distribution workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Deployment and warehouse process training are required.

recipes.title: Choose a self-hosted CRM
recipes.description: Compare configurable business records, prebuilt sales/service processes and developer-defined applications.

picks.label: Sales and service processes
picks.reason: Contacts, opportunities, quotations and service records support an established CRM workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Review the current 8.x compatibility and migration documentation.

picks.label: Custom entities and fields
picks.reason: A configurable data model and REST interface adapt customer records to a particular business.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced extensions and cloud hosting can add fees.

picks.label: CRM applications as code
picks.reason: Custom objects, workflows, SDK and CLI tooling fit a developer-owned CRM implementation.
picks.tradeoff: Enterprise files have commercial terms and customization needs technical ownership.

recipes.title: Issue invoices from your own server
recipes.description: Check the actual billing workflow, branding restrictions and local e-invoice obligations before moving customer data.

picks.label: Focused quotes and invoices
picks.reason: Customer records, templates, quotes and payment tracking cover a compact billing workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced automation and full accounting are outside its main scope.

picks.label: Recurring billing under MIT
picks.reason: Recurring invoices, contacts and payment links are available through a self-hosted application.
picks.tradeoff: Payment gateways and operational support have separate costs.

picks.label: Broader billing and client portal
picks.reason: Recurring invoices, expenses, payment gateways and desktop clients connect to a billing server.
picks.tradeoff: Elastic License restrictions and paid branding removal need review.

recipes.title: Keep small-business books under your control
recipes.description: Choose between an offline single-user program, a shared browser application and a larger ERP. Verify accounting localization against the business’s requirements.

picks.label: Offline single-user bookkeeping
picks.reason: The free desktop edition keeps accounting available without a subscription or network connection.
picks.tradeoff: Multi-user arrangements differ and the FSL includes a noncompete restriction.

picks.label: Self-hosted browser bookkeeping
picks.reason: The current Frappe application combines ledgers, invoices, stock and point-of-sale records.
picks.tradeoff: The previous Electron desktop application is end-of-life; the successor requires a server.

picks.label: Accounting within a full ERP
picks.reason: Financial records connect to purchasing, inventory and manufacturing workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Implementation effort is greater than a focused bookkeeping application.

recipes.title: Budget or account with local data
recipes.description: An envelope budget and a double-entry journal solve different problems; choose the data-entry model you will maintain consistently.

picks.label: Envelope budgeting
picks.reason: Local-first budgets and transaction imports support a planned allocation of personal spending.
picks.tradeoff: Bank-data integrations and hosted sync may incur separate costs.

picks.label: Versioned plain-text accounting
picks.reason: Text journals and scriptable reports make double-entry records inspectable and reproducible.
picks.tradeoff: Learning journal syntax and accounting rules takes commitment.

picks.label: Graphical double-entry accounts
picks.reason: A graphical accounting workflow is suitable when text journals are not the preferred entry method.
picks.tradeoff: Budgeting behavior differs from an envelope-first application.

recipes.title: Build internal business tools
recipes.description: Start with where the data lives and who maintains the tool: spreadsheet-style records, no-code databases or interfaces over existing services.

picks.label: Relational spreadsheets
picks.reason: Typed tables, Python formulas, linked views and access rules add structure to spreadsheet-style editing.
picks.tradeoff: Its relational document model differs from a conventional spreadsheet grid.

picks.label: No-code database applications
picks.reason: Tables, relationships, forms and an application builder support data-centered workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Premium and enterprise functionality have separate commercial licenses.

picks.label: Interfaces over existing systems
picks.reason: Widgets, database/API connectors and JavaScript build admin tools around current infrastructure.
picks.tradeoff: Queries, credentials and access controls require developer ownership.

recipes.title: Run a small-shop point of sale
recipes.description: Test the actual receipt printer, barcode reader, payment arrangement and local fiscal requirements before production use.

picks.label: Browser-based register
picks.reason: Item stock, customer records, receipts and sales reports can run on a local web server.
picks.tradeoff: Its MIT-derived license requires visible footer attribution, and peripherals need validation.

picks.label: Desktop till and back office
picks.reason: A desktop register with receipt layouts, barcode support and kitchen-display integration targets shop hardware.
picks.tradeoff: Recent maintenance was not established from the older release listing.

recipes.title: Choose a terminal workspace
recipes.description: Separate a terminal emulator from the shell it runs. Decide whether panes, remote sessions, configuration language or a minimal window matter most; GPU acceleration alone does not establish a performance winner.

picks.label: Integrated terminal workspace
picks.reason: Tabs, panes, multiplexing and Lua configuration support a multi-session terminal workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Its configuration and built-in session model take time to learn.

picks.label: Extensible Linux/macOS terminal
picks.reason: Kittens and keyboard-oriented terminal features support a configurable workstation.
picks.tradeoff: Native Windows support is not established.

picks.label: Platform-integrated terminal
picks.reason: Native desktop integration and terminal features suit supported macOS and Linux systems.
picks.tradeoff: Check platform feature differences and available package routes.

picks.label: Focused terminal window
picks.reason: A deliberately focused emulator works well with an external shell and multiplexer.
picks.tradeoff: Tabs and session management may require other tools.

recipes.title: Inspect and edit binary files
recipes.description: Choose between direct byte edits, reusable binary structures and a native desktop interface. Preserve an original copy before changing a file.

picks.label: Direct Windows hex editing
picks.reason: A Windows hex editor covers byte-level inspection and editing without requiring a template language.
picks.tradeoff: Structured parsing and cross-platform workflows need other choices.

picks.label: Reusable binary templates
picks.reason: Templates expose fields and structures in supported binary formats.
picks.tradeoff: It is commercial software and templates still require format knowledge.

picks.label: Pattern-driven binary analysis
picks.reason: A pattern language and visual analysis tools help inspect structured binary data.
picks.tradeoff: The broader analysis interface has a learning curve.

picks.label: Native macOS editor
picks.reason: A Mac-focused hex interface fits local inspection of large files.
picks.tradeoff: Its platform scope is macOS.

recipes.title: Choose a computational notebook workflow
recipes.description: Consider execution order, collaboration artifacts and the surrounding analysis workspace before choosing a notebook interface.

picks.label: Reactive Python notebooks
picks.reason: A dependency-aware execution model and Python source files help make state relationships explicit.
picks.tradeoff: Reactive behavior differs from a traditional manually executed notebook.

picks.label: Focused notebook interface
picks.reason: A familiar notebook document combines code, rich outputs and explanatory text.
picks.tradeoff: Execution state and cell order still require discipline.

picks.label: Larger analysis workspace
picks.reason: Notebooks, editors, terminals and extensions can share a workspace.
picks.tradeoff: Extensions and multiple tools increase environment-management work.

recipes.title: Choose a local SQL engine
recipes.description: Local transaction storage, file analytics and versioned relational tables are different needs. These tools overlap in SQL access but are not interchangeable database designs.

picks.label: Small local relational database
picks.reason: The CLI operates directly on SQLite files and can be scripted.
picks.tradeoff: SQLite concurrency and type behavior should fit the application.

picks.label: Analytical queries over local data
picks.reason: An in-process analytical engine suits SQL exploration of columnar and tabular files.
picks.tradeoff: It is not a replacement for every multi-user transactional service.

picks.label: Versioned relational data
picks.reason: Git-like table history supports branching and reviewing database changes.
picks.tradeoff: Its versioning and SQL compatibility require a representative trial.

recipes.title: Serve analytical or time-series data
recipes.description: Choose around query shape, ingestion, deployment scale and operational ownership. No common workload benchmark was run for this guide.

picks.label: General analytical service
picks.reason: A column-oriented database targets large analytical queries and aggregations.
picks.tradeoff: Running a shared service requires capacity, storage and upgrade planning.

picks.label: Timestamp-oriented ingestion
picks.reason: Its documented time-series features suit timestamped measurements and events.
picks.tradeoff: SQL and storage behavior differ from general-purpose transactional databases.

picks.label: Local analytical processing
picks.reason: An embedded engine can avoid operating a server for a single-user analytical task.
picks.tradeoff: A local embedded workflow does not provide the same shared-service architecture.

recipes.title: Browse databases with a GUI
recipes.description: Verify the actual database driver, authentication method and edition before choosing a client. A client does not replace the database service.

picks.label: Multiple database types
picks.reason: A database browser and query editor supports a mix of engines and local data work.
picks.tradeoff: Check each connector and any paid-edition feature requirements.

picks.label: Focused SQL desktop workflow
picks.reason: A query-and-table interface suits day-to-day SQL inspection.
picks.tradeoff: Community and commercial editions differ.

picks.label: Broad database ecosystem
picks.reason: Driver-based connections and data tools cover many database families.
picks.tradeoff: Its breadth creates more configuration and interface complexity.

recipes.title: Version database schema changes
recipes.description: Migration style, database support and current licensing matter more than the number of features on a product homepage. Test rollback and drift behavior on a representative schema.

picks.label: Plain SQL migrations
picks.reason: A compact CLI keeps migration files close to ordinary SQL.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced orchestration and governance need other systems.

picks.label: Ordered migration workflow
picks.reason: Versioned migrations fit a deployment pipeline with explicit sequence.
picks.tradeoff: Database coverage and advanced commands vary by edition.

picks.label: Structured changelogs
picks.reason: Changesets and changelog formats support explicit database-change history.
picks.tradeoff: Current Community uses FSL terms, and rollback is change-dependent.

picks.label: Desired-state schema planning
picks.reason: Declarative models can produce migration plans from a desired schema.
picks.tradeoff: Apache Community, standard binaries and Pro capabilities have different scope and terms.

recipes.title: Orchestrate data jobs
recipes.description: Compare the unit you want to manage: scheduled DAGs, Python flows, data assets or event-driven workflows. All require operational ownership beyond writing a task.

picks.label: Scheduled task DAGs
picks.reason: A mature DAG model and operator ecosystem suit scheduled batch pipelines.
picks.tradeoff: A production deployment has several services and scheduling concepts.

picks.label: Python flow control
picks.reason: Python flows and task state help add orchestration around existing Python work.
picks.tradeoff: Hosted services and self-managed deployments have different operations and pricing.

picks.label: Data-asset modeling
picks.reason: Asset-oriented orchestration makes produced datasets and dependencies visible.
picks.tradeoff: Adopting the asset model may require restructuring existing pipelines.

picks.label: Declarative event workflows
picks.reason: YAML workflow definitions and plugins connect jobs across systems.
picks.tradeoff: Plugin behavior and edition-specific capabilities need review.

recipes.title: Publish business intelligence reports
recipes.description: Distinguish browser-built dashboards from reports maintained as source code. Hosting, authentication and advanced governance may belong to a separate edition.

picks.label: Accessible browser exploration
picks.reason: A query and dashboard interface helps teams explore connected data.
picks.tradeoff: Embedding and governance features can be edition-dependent.

picks.label: Configurable analytical dashboards
picks.reason: SQL exploration, charts and dashboards fit an administered BI service.
picks.tradeoff: Deployment and semantic configuration require technical ownership.

picks.label: Reports as reviewed code
picks.reason: SQL, Markdown and reusable components suit versioned analytical reports.
picks.tradeoff: Hosted Studio capabilities are separate from the Core framework.

recipes.title: Choose a project test runner
recipes.description: Start with the language and build system. These runners belong to different ecosystems; compare features only after choosing the relevant ecosystem.

picks.label: Python tests and fixtures
picks.reason: Fixtures, assertions and plugins fit Python projects.
picks.tradeoff: Plugin compatibility and fixture design need maintenance.

picks.label: Vite-aligned JavaScript tests
picks.reason: A test runner integrated with the Vite ecosystem can share project configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Existing Jest behavior should be checked during migration.

picks.label: Established JavaScript suites
picks.reason: A broad JavaScript testing ecosystem supports existing Jest-based projects.
picks.tradeoff: Module-system and transformer configuration can be involved.

picks.label: Shell command behavior
picks.reason: Bash-based tests can assert command output and exit status.
picks.tradeoff: Shell portability still needs testing on the actual target environments.

recipes.title: Check code and automation files before running them
recipes.description: Use a checker that understands the file language. Static findings are useful evidence, but passing a linter does not establish runtime correctness or security.

picks.label: Python linting and formatting
picks.reason: Python-focused lint rules and formatting provide a combined local code-quality tool.
picks.tradeoff: Rule configuration and unsafe fixes require deliberate review.

picks.label: Shell-script diagnostics
picks.reason: Shell-aware analysis catches quoting and portability issues.
picks.tradeoff: It cannot validate every runtime input or external command.

picks.label: Dockerfile checks
picks.reason: Dockerfile rules and shell analysis support container build-file review.
picks.tradeoff: Image behavior and vulnerability status require separate checks.

picks.label: GitHub Actions definitions
picks.reason: Workflow syntax and expression checking catch errors before a hosted run.
picks.tradeoff: External action behavior and credentials are outside static validation.

recipes.title: Transform developer data locally
recipes.description: Compare isolated utility widgets with a chained transformation workflow. Confirm whether the chosen deployment executes data processing locally before using sensitive input.

picks.label: Individual developer utilities
picks.reason: A collection of encoders, converters and generators covers many small tasks.
picks.tradeoff: A selected hosted instance is distinct from self-hosting the application.

picks.label: Repeatable transformation recipes
picks.reason: Composable operations make decoding and conversion sequences inspectable.
picks.tradeoff: Recipes need validation against the actual input format; a successful decode is not proof of meaning.

recipes.title: Evaluate language-model applications
recipes.description: Separate automated evaluation from observing production traces and collecting human review data. Model-based scores need validation against the task you care about.

picks.label: Automated evaluation cases
picks.reason: A test-oriented evaluation library helps define repeatable checks for LLM behavior.
picks.tradeoff: Judge models, metric settings and API costs can affect results.

picks.label: Traces and evaluation context
picks.reason: Observability connects prompts, model calls and evaluation records.
picks.tradeoff: Running the platform and handling telemetry data require operational choices.

picks.label: Human review datasets
picks.reason: Configurable labeling interfaces support human evaluation tasks.
picks.tradeoff: Annotation design and reviewer agreement remain part of the methodology.

recipes.title: Label vision and text datasets
recipes.description: Select for annotation modality, export format and reviewer workflow. Verify what the self-hosted edition includes before assuming a hosted demo represents it.

picks.label: Visual annotation workflows
picks.reason: Image, video and point-cloud tools plus standard exports fit computer-vision labeling.
picks.tradeoff: Community requires an operated server and differs from Online and Enterprise.

picks.label: Configurable multi-modal tasks
picks.reason: Templates and configurable labeling interfaces adapt to varied annotation work.
picks.tradeoff: Complex workflows can require custom configuration and integration.

picks.label: Text and model feedback
picks.reason: Dataset fields and a Python SDK connect text review to programmatic workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Upstream limits ongoing work to maintenance rather than new feature development.

recipes.title: Transcribe media on your computer
recipes.description: Local inference requires the appropriate model files and hardware. Check language and audio quality on your own sample; no accuracy ranking is established here.

picks.label: Desktop transcription and subtitles
picks.reason: A GUI, watch folders and subtitle exports suit repeated media workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Choose the correct published architecture; v1.4.5 remains the last Intel Mac package.

picks.label: Scriptable local inference
picks.reason: A native implementation supports CLI and embedded transcription workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Model conversion, runtime options and integrations take technical setup.

recipes.title: Install and maintain game modlists
recipes.description: Start with the exact game and mod ecosystem. A modlist manager cannot promise compatibility between arbitrary lists or replace the author’s installation instructions.

picks.label: Curated list installations
picks.reason: Automated list installation helps reproduce an author-defined supported setup.
picks.tradeoff: Downloads, game versions and required third-party accounts must match the list.

picks.label: Thunderstore game profiles
picks.reason: Profiles and dependency handling fit supported Thunderstore communities.
picks.tradeoff: It does not cover every game or mod distribution site.

recipes.title: Choose a game mod loader
recipes.description: The game and runtime decide which loader is applicable. These are ecosystem-specific foundations rather than interchangeable tools for every game.

picks.label: Stardew Valley mods
picks.reason: A game-specific API and loader connect supported Stardew Valley mods.
picks.tradeoff: Game and mod versions must be compatible with the installed SMAPI release.

picks.label: Supported Unity games
picks.reason: A loader and framework support mods for compatible Unity runtimes.
picks.tradeoff: Compatibility varies by game and anti-cheat or online policy.

picks.label: Executable-specific mod setups
picks.reason: A launcher and loader organize configurations for supported PC games.
picks.tradeoff: Each mod and game has its own setup and compatibility requirements.

recipes.title: Organize an emulation library
recipes.description: Distinguish a frontend that launches other software from a framework that also manages emulator cores. Neither provides game files or guarantees a particular game runs.

picks.label: Configured desktop collection
picks.reason: A desktop frontend organizes game metadata, themes and launch commands.
picks.tradeoff: Emulators and legally obtained game files must be configured separately; Android terms differ.

picks.label: Theme-driven launcher
picks.reason: A customizable frontend can unify games and applications under metadata definitions.
picks.tradeoff: Theme and launch configuration take manual work.

picks.label: Core-based emulation interface
picks.reason: A shared frontend provides settings and controls across supported emulator cores.
picks.tradeoff: Compatibility depends on the selected core and its requirements.

recipes.title: Inspect graphics API frames
recipes.description: Select by graphics API, operating system and GPU. Capturing a frame is a development or debugging workflow, not a promise to increase frame rate.

picks.label: Cross-vendor frame capture
picks.reason: A frame debugger exposes graphics API calls and resources on supported APIs.
picks.tradeoff: Supported APIs and capture environments must match the application.

picks.label: Trace and replay API calls
picks.reason: Trace/replay tools help inspect a sequence of graphics calls.
picks.tradeoff: The workflow and API coverage differ from a full vendor profiler.

picks.label: DirectX on Windows
picks.reason: Microsoft’s tooling supports DirectX analysis on Windows.
picks.tradeoff: Its platform and API scope are specific; licensing was not fully classified.

picks.label: NVIDIA graphics analysis
picks.reason: Vendor tooling provides graphics debugging and profiling for supported NVIDIA hardware.
picks.tradeoff: Driver, GPU and API requirements must be checked.

recipes.title: Choose a build orchestrator
recipes.description: Build graphs, language rules and cache infrastructure matter more than a generic speed claim. Compare using the project’s real dependency graph.

picks.label: Explicit multi-language build graph
picks.reason: Declared targets and toolchains support cached and reproducible build workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Rule ecosystems and dependency declarations require investment.

picks.label: Large dependency-graph workflows
picks.reason: A modern build engine targets incremental execution and programmable rules.
picks.tradeoff: Adoption requires compatible rules, toolchains and project migration.

picks.label: Python-defined builds
picks.reason: Python build descriptions fit projects needing programmable build logic.
picks.tradeoff: Its execution and cache model differ from remote-build-oriented systems.

recipes.title: Run a local web development stack
recipes.description: Decide whether the project primarily needs containers with web services or a shell containing language tools. Docker-provider terms and resource use remain separate.

picks.label: PHP and CMS development
picks.reason: Documented local HTTPS, databases, Xdebug and quickstarts support common CMS projects.
picks.tradeoff: Requires a supported Docker provider and is primarily a development environment.

picks.label: Custom service recipes
picks.reason: A Landofile combines application recipes, services and project commands.
picks.tradeoff: Plugins and Docker configuration must match the team environment.

picks.label: Toolchain-oriented shell
picks.reason: A JSON declaration installs project tools through Nix.
picks.tradeoff: It does not automatically provide the same container-service topology.

recipes.title: Choose project environment control
recipes.description: Variable loading, tool installation and reproducible package builds are separate layers. Several of these tools can be used together.

picks.label: Automatic project variables
picks.reason: Approved environment settings load and unload with directory changes.
picks.tradeoff: It executes authorized shell code and does not install a full toolchain itself.

picks.label: Declared tools with simpler configuration
picks.reason: A JSON package list creates a Nix-backed project shell.
picks.tradeoff: Package behavior and Windows WSL requirements still apply.

picks.label: Detailed package and build control
picks.reason: Declarative dependency models support reproducible shells and custom packages.
picks.tradeoff: Its packaging language and store model take more learning.

picks.label: Language tool versions and tasks
picks.reason: A project-oriented manager coordinates common developer tool versions and tasks.
picks.tradeoff: Backend and tool-specific installation behavior needs checking.

recipes.title: Build a data-driven internal app
recipes.description: Choose around the main artifact: editable database records, an analytical report, or a visually assembled application. Authentication and database access remain explicit design work.

picks.label: SQL-defined forms and pages
picks.reason: Queries can produce data-entry forms, tables and charts with a small server.
picks.tradeoff: Application permissions and validation must be designed carefully.

picks.label: Analytical narrative and metrics
picks.reason: SQL and Markdown reports combine explanation with reusable analytical components.
picks.tradeoff: It is report-oriented; Studio features have separate scope.

picks.label: Visual application assembly
picks.reason: Widgets and data connections support internal tool interfaces.
picks.tradeoff: Edition limits and the hosted/self-managed deployment model must fit the project.

recipes.title: Choose an integrated JavaScript runtime
recipes.description: Evaluate an existing application, its native dependencies and deployment target before replacing a runtime. This is a documented-feature comparison, not a universal speed ranking.

picks.label: Explicit permissions and TypeScript tooling
picks.reason: Runtime permissions and built-in development commands suit controlled TypeScript execution.
picks.tradeoff: Node compatibility and permission settings need testing on the actual application.

picks.label: Runtime plus package and build tools
picks.reason: A single toolkit combines JavaScript execution, dependencies, bundling and tests.
picks.tradeoff: Check Node/native-module compatibility and the required CPU/platform build.

recipes.title: Manage JavaScript project dependencies
recipes.description: Package-manager choice affects lockfiles, install scripts and CI behavior. Keep one deliberate project policy and validate changes with the actual dependency tree.

picks.label: Standard Node package workflow
picks.reason: The bundled CLI offers package scripts, workspaces and locked CI installation.
picks.tradeoff: Registry services have separate terms from the open-source CLI.

picks.label: Shared package-store workflow
picks.reason: A content-addressed store and workspace tooling suit many multi-project setups.
picks.tradeoff: Dependencies that assume a flat installation may need fixes.

picks.label: Configurable resolution and workspaces
picks.reason: Modern Yarn offers plugins, constraints and Plug’n’Play or node_modules strategies.
picks.tradeoff: Modern Yarn and Classic differ; migration needs compatibility checks.

picks.label: Integrated toolkit adoption
picks.reason: Its package manager can be evaluated alongside the runtime and test tools.
picks.tradeoff: Adopting one component does not prove the entire toolkit fits a project.

recipes.title: Choose a version-control working style
recipes.description: Compare a new change model, a conventional Git GUI and a complete repository/project system. Their storage and collaboration semantics differ.

picks.label: Git-backed change editing
picks.reason: Automatic snapshots, operation history and descendant rebasing suit stacked-change workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Higher-level metadata and bookmark semantics differ from ordinary Git.

picks.label: Conventional Git with a GUI
picks.reason: Diff, staging and history controls work on ordinary local Git repositories.
picks.tradeoff: It changes the interface rather than replacing Git’s underlying model.

picks.label: Integrated project history
picks.reason: Source control, tickets, wiki and forum can travel in one self-hosted system.
picks.tradeoff: The repository format and collaboration workflow differ from Git.

recipes.title: Back up PC game saves
recipes.description: Choose discovery and automation separately, verify a representative restore, and keep a backup copy outside the original disk. Neither application guarantees every game’s save format transfers between systems.

picks.label: Cross-store scan and portable backups
picks.reason: A game manifest, custom entries and a CLI support manual or scripted save backups.
picks.tradeoff: Verify detected paths and restore behavior for each important game.

picks.label: Backup after game exit
picks.reason: Process monitoring can create compressed save history after playing.
picks.tradeoff: Supported process definitions and paths must be configured; macOS is not documented.

recipes.title: Adjust a game’s rendering workflow
recipes.description: Choose by the exact visual problem and supported game/API. Review multiplayer and anti-cheat restrictions before using injected tools.

picks.label: Presentation, HDR and pacing controls
picks.reason: A game modification framework exposes HDR, display and frame-pacing adjustments.
picks.tradeoff: Per-game compatibility and stable/experimental differences matter; no general speed gain is promised.

picks.label: Post-processing shaders
picks.reason: A shader injector supports a customizable post-processing pipeline.
picks.tradeoff: Game/API compatibility and online restrictions still apply.

recipes.title: Prepare installation and recovery USB media
recipes.description: Choose by the machine preparing the drive, the image type and whether one drive must hold several installers. These are documented workflow fits; no firmware compatibility or write-speed comparison was performed.

picks.label: Windows host with boot-setting controls
picks.reason: Use when a Windows PC needs to prepare installation media with explicit BIOS/UEFI and image options.
picks.tradeoff: Writing erases the selected destination; the image and target hardware still need compatibility checks.

picks.label: Several boot images on one drive
picks.reason: Use when maintaining a portable library of installers or rescue images that can be copied onto a prepared drive.
picks.tradeoff: Initial preparation reformats the drive; image, Secure Boot and firmware behavior varies.

picks.label: Straightforward image flashing across desktop systems
picks.reason: Use when the main task is writing and validating an existing disk image on Windows, macOS or Linux.
picks.tradeoff: It is an image writer; advanced installer customization and multi-image boot menus require other tools.

picks.label: Raspberry Pi setup
picks.reason: Use when selecting a Raspberry Pi operating system and preparing its storage through the official setup workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Its configuration options serve Raspberry Pi deployment rather than every PC installer.

recipes.title: Choose a partition-management workflow
recipes.description: Separate offline partition layout work, everyday Linux disk administration and a combined Windows disk utility. Backups and a verified destination matter because these operations change stored data.

picks.label: Offline layout changes
